title: The person usually credited with it isn't who built it first.
description:
The person usually credited with it isn't who built it first. Infinite scroll is one of the most copied interface patterns in software history, and the popular story about its origin is a year off, and about the wrong team.

A Microsoft search engineering lead. He and two colleagues, Julie Farago and Nick Craswell, built the feature into MSN's image search after data showed testers paging through dozens of results rather than stop, one went to around page twenty before clicking a photo of a chocolate cake.

Microsoft's patent for it predates the famous version by a year. Filed 14 February 2006, naming Farago, Williams and a colleague as inventors. The programmer usually credited with inventing infinite scroll built his own version at a different company in 2006, after this one had already shipped.

The hard limit Microsoft actually built into its 'infinite' scroll. It was never truly infinite, just longer than anyone expected to reach.

The feature everyone recognises. The credit almost nobody has right.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_scrolling - read in full 1 Sep 2026: infinite scroll was filed as a patent application on 14 February 2006 by Microsoft's Windows Live (MSN) Search image team; the feature shipped in the team's image search on 8 March 2006, the first product to ship with it; Microsoft engineering lead Hugh Williams has stated that he, Julie Farago and Nick Craswell were the inventors; Aza Raskin separately claimed credit for inventing infinite scroll in 2019.
- https://hughewilliams.com/2012/03/06/ideas-and-invention-and-the-story-of-bings-image-search/ - read in full 1 Sep 2026, first-person account by named co-inventor Hugh Williams: he, Nick Craswell and Julie Farago built the feature into MSN Search's image results in 2005 after session data showed that while about 75% of web-search queries stayed on page one, only about 43% of image-search queries did, with some users paging into the twenties before clicking a result (his own example: a user who clicked a photo of a chocolate cake on roughly page twenty-something); the internal build was capped at 1,000 images, so it was never actually infinite.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aza_Raskin - read in full 1 Sep 2026: confirms Raskin's career timeline (born 1984; founded Humanized in 2005 after his father Jef Raskin's death); the article documents Raskin's other credited work, such as the tabnabbing phishing technique, but does not itself credit him with infinite scroll, consistent with the Infinite Scrolling article crediting Microsoft's team instead.
